entries.title: Trump’s Kennedy Center Shakedown
entries.summary: The only appropriate response is to refuse to accede to his demands.
entries.content:
The only appropriate response is to refuse to accede to his demands.

The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will not go away. In May, Trump lost in court and was ordered to remove his name from the building. But now—according to a 57-page presentation by Trump’s hand-picked executive board obtained by The Washington Post—the Kennedy Center is warning that it will likely go bankrupt. Unless, that is, Trump gets to put his name back on the wall next to that of his slain predecessor.

The Post reports:

Trump’s support hinges on getting public credit for his involvement. The financial resolution says Trump has offered to “raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy” while the building undergoes a sweeping renovation. But it says Trump is unlikely to provide “fundamental oversight” of that project or lead a financial rescue without “appropriate recognition” of his role.

That’s not an offer of help; it’s a shakedown—or, in more direct terms, political blackmail. Two lawyers who have been fighting the Trump administration, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement: “Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way.” The president is counting on the board’s civic spirit and affection for the institution—neither of which he evidently possesses—to strong-arm it into giving him what the law and courts would not allow.

Even more galling than Trump’s attempt to pressure the trustees is that his offer is a response to a crisis mostly of his own creation. It’s true that the Kennedy Center, opened more than a half century ago, needs investment and repairs. But the plummeting ticket sales are a result of Trump’s hostile takeover. Performers and patrons alike did not want to legitimize the obscenity of placing Trump’s name on an institution meant to honor Kennedy, and they voted with their feet and their dollars. This very public repudiation of Trump by a slice of the American cultural elite appears to have been an embarrassment to the president; Trump then claimed that he needed to close the center for two years (ostensibly for a complete reconstruction) rather than suffer further humiliation.

(Trump, apparently, could not submit to the public indignity of having his name removed from the building in June. He—or someone seeking to please him—ordered workers to cover the building’s wall with tarps at 3 o’clock in the morning so that no one would see the removal. The tarps remain in place.)

The only way to avert letting the center go bankrupt, according to the executive board, is to let Trump raise money—and heaven knows what kind of ethical issues that effort would entail—and then to add his name to thank him. The presentation to the board suggests 10 possible statements to place on the building, including “Renovation Restoration and Endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Putting Trump’s name in front of Kennedy’s is an especially offensive touch, and would enshrine the idea that the center would no longer be named solely for Kennedy.

The American people do not support Trump’s mania for renaming things, of which the Kennedy Center is just one example. (The White House itself has become a public exhibit of Trump’s garish taste, including gold script identifying The Oval Office, as if it’s a function room at one of his resorts that needs to be labeled in case a tipsy wedding guest gets lost.) All of this architectural bombast and glitz are expressions both of ego and of insecurity: Trump wants to leave his mark—and his name—on a city that has never accepted him and that will almost certainly try to scrub away his influence when he is gone.

The president admitted as much recently, when the writer Ben Terris asked him whether he is building monuments to himself because he is worried that no one else will build them when he’s gone. “That’s true,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.”

The president’s admission suggests a way to deal with his attempted shakedown of the Kennedy Center board: take his dare.

The center’s top officials, the people who were supposed to be entrusted with the future of this cultural icon, have admitted their failure. They acknowledge that Trump will not support the institution unless his name is on it. Well, so be it. The trustees should let the center close, declare bankruptcy, and come to a sad end—all on Trump’s watch. Allow the Kennedy Center to fail in full view of the American public, and let them decide whether such things matter.

Otherwise, Trump will plow ahead and do something no one wants, because no one bothered to stop him.

The Kennedy Center can always be rebuilt and reopened. Indeed, the restoration of the center could be one of the items on the next president’s to-do list. Scrap the czarist-style ballroom. Rebuild the East Wing of the White House. Halt the fascist-flavored victory arch that will dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery. Fix the Reflecting Pool. Chisel Trump’s name off the U.S. Institute of Peace. (If the president wants to land at Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach when he leaves office, that’s between him and the people of Florida.) Painful as it would be to see the Kennedy Center go bankrupt, it would be more painful to cave to Trump’s deeply cynical refusal to save a national treasure unless he gets his name on it.

In a famous 1911 poem that gave the world another name for blackmail—danegeld, a reference to the protection money that medieval English villages paid, often in vain, to Danish raiders—Rudyard Kipling warned powerful countries against caving to extortionary threats. The Kennedy Center board, and the American people, should heed Kipling’s advice:

We never pay any-one Dane-geld,

No matter how trifling the cost;

For the end of that game is oppression and shame,

And the nation that plays it is lost!

entries.title: A Bigoted Outburst Against Texas Sports Fans
entries.summary: Bo French’s xenophobia should force Republicans to confront the prejudice in their ranks.
entries.content:
Bo French’s xenophobia should force Republicans to confront the prejudice in their ranks.

On Saturday night, college-football fans in Texas were blessed with a moment of collective ecstasy. Their Longhorns were playing Ohio State, the nation’s No. 1 team, and trailed by 20 points. Then they improbably scored three touchdowns in the fourth quarter. A frenzy shook the stadium as more than 100,000 people, most in team colors, celebrated the stunning comeback. But Bo French, the Republican nominee for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, was upset by what he saw in the crowd.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” he wrote yesterday on X, where he posted an image of a cluster of fans at the stadium who appeared to be of South Asian ancestry. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” Dispelling any doubts about his meaning, he continued: “I weep for the families in Texas who can’t get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans.” He added, “Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners.”

In reality, there is no reason to assume that the students in the photograph are foreigners, and Texas does not prioritize foreigners over Texans. Quite the contrary. Ninety percent of slots for first-year students at UT Austin are reserved for Texas residents. Foreign students even pay higher tuition, which effectively acts as a subsidy for Texas residents at the college. But some people are so psychologically distressed by diversity and difference that their reactions have little to do with the facts on the ground.

Some prominent Republicans have objected to the latest––but not the only––bigoted remarks from French. Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who has held office since 2002, posted on X, “Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized.” He warned, “This is how great political parties self destruct.”

But others seemed more incensed by Cornyn’s critique than they were by French’s remarks. A Republican state legislator from North Dakota wrote, “Eat shit you fucking loser.” John Doyle, who has a show for the populist-right outlet Blaze Media, wrote, “For now we can ignore how unqualified you are to speak on behalf of ‘The Republican Party’ as someone who reflexively embraces liberal moralizing about ‘racism’ and ‘intolerance’ in response to a Patriot acknowledging that Texans didn’t ask for their state to become a playground for the third world.”

Changes to content moderation on X under Elon Musk’s ownership––not to mention rhetoric and actions within the federal government––have made clear how common bigoted identitarianism is in the GOP coalition. Republicans who believe in the values of Christianity, the creed of the Declaration of Independence, or the moral imperative to judge people as individuals need to confront the prejudice in their ranks.

The identitarian right’s rise has lessons for progressives too. First, seeking to raise the salience of race and ethnicity in American politics and culture was a mistake––as ought to have been clear by 2016, when Donald Trump exploited that heightened salience for his own ends. As the political scientist Karen Stenner argued in her 2005 book, causing people who are uncomfortable with difference to perceive it as a threat to social cohesion can activate a latent predisposition toward intolerance.

Second, not only was embracing race as a factor in university admissions unpopular with voters, so much so that it lost ballot initiatives even in left-leaning California; colleges’ discrimination against white people and Asians also stoked racial resentment by putting identity groups in a zero-sum competition.

And third, once the left began to treat mere departures from left-identitarian shibboleths as racist, it became harder to stigmatize actual racism or xenophobia, as surely as crying wolf at every shih tzu, tabby cat, and hamster would make it harder to warn against actual wolves on the hunt.

The Republican and Democratic Parties could do well in future elections to revive a straightforward, morally sound position: Judge others by the content of their character, not by the color of their skin. That ethos needn’t foreclose all disagreements about immigration. And one needn’t pretend not to notice racial and ethnic diversity. But insofar as a diverse crowd cheering for a Longhorn victory implies anything about past or present immigration and its effects, it is this: People of all races and ethnicities have already assimilated into the quasi-religion of Texas football, one of America’s most distinctive cultural phenomena.

If, heaven forbid, this great multiethnic nation is ever invaded by a foreign power, there is evidence that the people in that Texas stadium could unite in common cause without regard to race or ancestry. Bo French, who feels distress at seeing his neighbors come together, may lack that ability––a weakness that makes him unfit for office in America.

entries.title: Gas Prices Could Cost Republicans the Midterms
entries.summary: Many voters understand that the president isn’t directly responsible for the price of oil. Except this time, he is.
entries.content:
Many voters understand that the president isn’t directly responsible for the price of oil. Except this time, he is.

One might expect Donald Trump to be concerned about gas prices. Less than two months out from the midterms, gas costs 37 percent more than it did a year ago. Home-heating oil was up 52 percent as of August, and diesel is up a staggering 69 percent. None of those numbers is likely to go down significantly as long as the Iran war drags on. Meanwhile, just last week, a Saudi oil pipeline that carries about 4 percent of the global oil supply shut down after being bombed. (No one has claimed credit for the attack.)

But Trump says he isn’t worried. Speaking with reporters last week, he insisted that the United States, not Iran, is in control of the Strait of Hormuz. “Right after the election,” he said, “oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”

Even if that prediction were based on anything resembling fact, the timing would be too late to do Trump much good. Political scientists tend to agree that gas prices influence voter behavior. Although many voters no doubt understand that the president isn’t usually directly responsible for the price of oil, this time, he is. In fact, the oil shock related to Trump’s war of choice with Iran is the only reason the U.S. has any inflation to speak of. Inflation in all non-energy consumer purchases is at just 2 percent over the past year. If Democrats manage to take back the House and Senate in November despite an inhospitable electoral map, the Trump effect on gas prices may well be the reason.

Voters hate inflation, and gas prices are especially hard to tune out. Juan Felipe Riaño, an economist who has studied inflation’s political consequences, told me that voters understand that price increases translate into lower real wages. The more they drive, the more pronounced the effect. People who live in rural areas and exurbs have the most to lose, because they have the longest commutes. These are the reddest parts of the country, meaning that they are home to millions of voters whom Democrats are trying to persuade to vote blue. According to a Brookings Institution analysis, the average voter in a Republican-held district drives 26 percent more miles than their counterpart in a Democratic district. Other research has found that those with longer drive times are more likely to hold the president accountable for increases in gas prices.

These Trump-friendly areas are exactly where Democrats need to make inroads. They can’t take the Senate without winning multiple states that Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024. Meanwhile, although gerrymandering has created more red districts, it has done so by spreading the Republican advantage more thinly across districts. This has created more places where Democrats could win in a wave election. Currently, Democrats lead Republicans on generic congressional polls by about seven points. In a plus-seven election, their best recruits could pick up seats even in districts that went heavily for Trump in 2024.

Perhaps the best thing Trump could do to avoid that outcome would be to bring gas prices down before Election Day. His approval rating has been declining almost continuously since he took office a second time, and since August, it has hovered around 38 percent, according to Silver Bulletin. Voters say that their top issue is the cost of living, and only 25 percent approve of how Trump has handled it. That’s a decline of nine points since the war with Iran began.

As for Republican candidates in competitive races, their best bet for avoiding the gas-price backlash might be to distance themselves from the president. But Trump has made that extremely difficult. Last week, Republicans gathered in Dallas for an unusual midterm convention devoted to celebrating Trump’s greatness. At one point, he asked the crowd to repeat a “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States.”

And if Trump’s goal is to remind Republican candidates that their voters’ first loyalty is to him, not them, he seems to be succeeding. Only a tiny handful of congressional Republicans have publicly denounced the Iran war. Several vulnerable Republicans have refused to allow daylight between themselves and Trump, even when doing so would seem to be tactically wise. Michael Whatley, Mike Collins, and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominees in the swing states of North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan, respectively, all spoke at the convention. So, too, did Jon Husted and Ken Paxton, who are running in Ohio and Texas, two states Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024, but where polls suggest that Democrats have a chance to pick up Senate seats.

Even when voters believe that the president is to blame for painful gas-price increases, they may be unsure about how aligned their local House or Senate candidate is with the White House. Heading into the midterms, Trump is going out of his way to make sure no such uncertainty exists.

entries.title: Who Needs Regulation When Trump Is President?
entries.summary: The president is turning the charge of personalism into a promise.
entries.content:
The president is turning the charge of personalism into a promise.

One consistent complaint against the Trump administration is that it is imposing personalist rule, in which the whims of the leader override the law. Now Donald Trump has come out forcefully against regulating artificial intelligence—and his argument is based almost explicitly on the superiority of his omniscience over any formal legal process. He is not so much refuting the charge of personalism as turning it into a promise.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote in a self-refuting post on Truth Social.

Even the most market-friendly economist will concede that government intervention is required when any private activity creates an “externality”—that is, a cost imposed on people who are not involved in a transaction. A factory dumping toxic waste into a stream has heretofore provided the textbook case of an externality necessitating regulation. But AI bots destroying human civilization—as executives are warning could happen—clearly represents a much costlier externality. This is, in fact, probably the strongest conceivable case for regulation.

The intense competitive pressure among AI firms, which have a much stronger incentive to innovate quickly than to ensure their innovations are safe, enhances the case further.

Skeptics have valid reasons to worry about poorly designed regulation that either entrenches the current industry leaders or permits Chinese AI to overtake the American version. Those are reasons to demand well-designed regulations, not to avoid any rules at all.

Against this overwhelming rationale, Trump offers, in place of any neutral standards, his characteristic faith in his own prerogatives. Trump tends to discount the need for laws even in areas where he favors government action. He opposed congressional authorization for war with Iran. He has not asked Congress to levy tariffs, preferring instead to raise or lower them and provide carve-outs to affected firms based on his whim.

If anyone needs it, the incumbent president’s behavior provides excellent evidence against personalist rule in general and, in the case of AI, specifically. For one thing, his decisions are not necessarily aligned with the public interest. Trump has formed a political alliance with a handful of wealthy men who have a strong personal stake in the development and shape of AI. The dual roles of David Sacks, Trump’s most important AI adviser and an investor in AI, have caused even some White House officials to express concern about conflicts of interest.

Additionally, Trump has a long-standing tendency to focus on short-term concerns over long-term ones. Trump’s preference for immediate gratification explains many of his decisions, including defunding scientific and medical research, accelerating fossil-fuel emissions, and denigrating American soft power globally. Pushing forward AI development delivers financial benefits to Trump allies who have plied his party with donations. Trump seems to believe that the AI build-out is driving the economy at the moment. It is difficult to imagine any long-term concern persuading Trump to forgo the short-term benefits of the AI boom.

Finally, on the IQ point, Trump is correct that a high level of analytic intelligence is necessary to regulate wisely. This is not, however, a reason to empower Donald Trump. Although he possesses a distinct animal cunning and an uncanny sense for human weakness, Trump isn’t the type to dig in and understand new problems in all of their complexity. He does not appear to read texts of any length or substance, and he is reportedly unable to tolerate briefings of any depth. His public remarks are rambling and error-filled, and rely on a shrinking pool of vocabulary terms.

Trump does have expertise in a handful of realms, such as construction, entertainment, and men’s discount shoeware. Artificial intelligence and technology in general are not among his fields of specialization.

There are many reasons the United States needs clear, stable regulations on artificial intelligence, rather than relying on the whims of a leader. That is true even if the leader is public-minded and deeply versed in policy intricacies. It is all the more true if the leader is Donald Trump.

entries.title: Why Does Donald Trump Hate This Sculpture?
entries.summary: The president wants the Smithsonian to add a colossal George Washington statue—and remove another work of abstract art in D.C.
entries.content:
The president wants the Smithsonian to add a colossal George Washington statue—and remove another work of abstract art in D.C.

The sculpture that Donald Trump wants removed from the National Mall has a reputation even among its admirers for being a bit inscrutable. Dedicated in 1967 at what is now the National Museum of American History, José de Rivera’s Infinity looks, fittingly, like an infinity symbol with an extra twist. (A bow? A pretzel?) By pairing the technical prowess required to create smooth, curved metal with the delicate spinning of a music box, the slow-turning work seems to take a different form each time you pass it. The museum’s architect, Walker O. Cain, wrote that Infinity “has the characteristic of stimulating everyone who has seen it to create his own personal imaginative interpretation.”

But the president does not appear to have been stimulated. “That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday night. Trump insisted that the Smithsonian replace Infinity with a 30-foot high “Colossus” of George Washington. In the same post, he called for the mounting of a five-year exhibition about the Founding Father to open immediately (museum shows of such magnitude typically take years to plan), and said the museum should create a “Center for American Heroes.” Trump also wrote that the institution should add another, 11-foot-tall Washington statue to the museum’s Flag Hall. That one was displayed at the Grand Prix race held in Washington, D.C., this summer as part of Trump’s Freedom 250 festivities. He’d like it dedicated at the museum this Thursday.

Trump’s latest demands might be partially understood as a test of how far he can push an institution that he does not control. They came just three days after the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch, announced his upcoming retirement, following a year and a half of standing between the museum complex and the White House. In a July executive order, the president called on the National Park Service, which is part of the executive branch, to place signs outside the National Museum of American History accusing it of partisan bias.

Few would question the appropriateness of having a healthy amount of George Washington in an American-history museum, but Trump’s ask might be a little too redundant. For one thing, a Washington sculpture can already be found on the museum’s second floor. Classical in style and portraying the first president as a kind of Zeus figure, Horatio Greenough’s 1841 statue boasts chiseled muscles that rival even the machismo AI depictions Trump circulates of himself and Washington online. And when approached from the east, Rivera’s Infinity—the aspirational site of Trump’s Washington colossus—elegantly frames another abstract form: the obelisk known as the Washington Monument.

Trump’s call for changes to the museum fits a few recent patterns: He has been on a campaign to institute his preferred version of history in the national museum system. He has begun to leave his mark, and occasionally his name, across the architectural landscape of Washington, D.C. And while doing so, he appears to have indicated a distaste for abstract art. Earlier this month, the Kennedy Center, which Trump controls, took down Joel Shapiro’s playful metal sculpture Blue. When the Trump administration—addressing a controversy at the National Portrait Gallery last year—criticized a decidedly representational Amy Sherald painting of a trans woman as Lady Liberty, part of its complaint was that, in the words of the administration, “the Statue of Liberty is not an abstract canvas for political expression.” The use of abstract reads like an insult.

Trump has pushed a classical makeover in D.C.. He has issued executive orders mandating classical designs as the default for new federal buildings, for example, and remounted figurative statues that were torn down during the Black Lives Matter movement. He has mused about the White House upgrading its columns to a higher Greek order (adding more classical to the neoclassical); his most prized project, the White House ballroom, looks like a Corinthian-columned department store. In his first executive order on architecture, he said federal buildings should command respect.

When it comes to the Rivera outside the National Museum of American History, Trump’s issue with it—and with abstraction largely—might not be that the sculpture “says nothing about America,” but that it doesn’t say what he wants it to. That is, he can’t control what it says at all.

The American artist Robert Motherwell wrote in a 1951 essay celebrating abstraction that one of the most striking aspects of the approach is its “nakedness,” or the way it turns, with such decisiveness, away from the symbols we know. “How many rejections on the part of her artists! Whole worlds—the world of objects, the world of power and propaganda, the world of anecdotes, the world of fetishes and ancestor worship,” he wrote. With abstract works such as Infinity, we’re free to find our own reading—or not.

Whereas abstraction attempts to reject passed-down meanings, the image of George Washington is layered with them. Part of what is so moving about, say, getting up close to Washington’s military uniform at the National Museum of American History is the way it challenges how we’ve come to see him as an icon rather than as an actual person.

Abstraction has long been subject to right-wing attacks. During the Red Scare, for instance, George A. Dondero, a U.S. representative from Michigan, crusaded to rid American art of what he saw as communist influence. In a 1949 speech that could be ripped from Truth Social today, he framed a list of 20th-century art movements as un-American weapons for destruction: “Dadaism aims to destroy by ridicule. Expressionism aims to destroy by aping the primitive and insane,” he said. “Abstractionism aims to destroy by the creation of brainstorms.”

Sure, the unpredictable responses to abstract art—the brainstorms—can be a little intimidating. How many of us have stood, a bit clueless, before Jackson Pollock’s riotous colors or Cy Twombly’s frenetic scratches and wondered if we might need a Ph.D. for this?

But there’s also a certain joy to find in it. One National Museum of American History curator, David Shayt, embraced the compounding, shifting meanings of abstraction in a 2008 essay about the museum’s Rivera. The sculpture marked an early work of abstract art commissioned by the U.S. government, but, Shayt argues, the commission was more about the government’s belief that Rivera, a prominent abstract-expressionist sculptor known for his twisting metal forms, could capture the museum’s dual identity in its early days as the National Museum of History and Technology. Cain, the architect, had convinced the government that the sculpture would be a mechanical model of the solar system, a “twenty-first-century orrery.” But Rivera, who cited the abstractionist Piet Mondrian and the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși as among his influences, asserted no such thing. “What I make represents nothing but itself,” he said.

That didn’t stop the National Museum of American History’s staff from making their own meaning over the years, particularly as employees of a “pragmatic museum of history rather than a museum of art,” Shayt wrote. “Is it a mathematical symbol? A wisp of battlefield smoke? A tennis stroke?” he asked of Infinity. One of the sculpture’s greatest attributes, he continued, is “an expressiveness that can evolve in step with the evolution of the museum whose entrance it fronts.”

For an example of the kind of aesthetic Trump prefers, you don’t have to go far from the Rivera. A short walk brings you to Freedom Plaza, where the National Park Service has installed a pop-up exhibition for the nation’s 250th birthday. Rows of traditional, metal statues of Revolutionary War soldiers line the plaza—many, notably, represent enslaved individuals. Standing on a high plinth, meanwhile, is Caesar Rodney, a slaveholder and Declaration of Independence signer, who looms over the display. The statue had been removed in Delaware during the Black Lives Matter protests, only to be restored in Washington as some conservatives began championing him as a symbol of the left’s overreach. Trump has placed a similar style of traditional statue—direct, simple—throughout the White House Rose Garden and envisions much of the same for the Garden of American Heroes, another of his planned D.C. projects, where abstraction is explicitly forbidden. There’s very little room for interpretation in these sorts of statues. They mean what they mean.

Much of the Trump-era fight over history has boiled down to a struggle about trust. The Trump administration says the history the Smithsonian tells is not patriotic enough; the institution counters that Americans can hold patriotism and complexity at once. The National Museum of American History museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, told a congressional committee this summer: “Telling our history fully is not anti-American. It is a form of respect for the American people.” Abstraction, too, holds a kind of esteem for its viewers, trusting them to navigate its symbol-less terrain. In his essay, Motherwell wrote that the emergence of abstract art is one sign that there are still people who “know how to respect and follow their inner feelings, no matter how irrational or absurd they may first appear.”

On the west side of the museum stands another abstract piece, a massive, 40-foot Alexander Calder that the museum calls a “monument to modernity.” Its jagged black edges reach outward, conveying a sense of rupture or change. On Saturday, the area around the Calder was roped off with caution tape, surely something to do with conservation or work on the museum grounds. But it felt a little ominous, as though it were a warning not for museumgoers, but for the art itself.

entries.title: A Nation of Strange, Idle Men
entries.summary: Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.
entries.content:
Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.

Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West—primarily because of his music, but also because of his unique position as the one celebrity who seemed empowered to behave however he wanted. He interrupted Taylor Swift at the Video Music Awards; he said “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people” at a Hurricane Katrina fundraiser; he brought a Jesus look-alike onstage. I would shrug, and keep listening. Then his do what I want ethos went very bad. Ye called slavery “a choice”; he came out as a fan of Hitler; he wore a KKK-style hood.

With escalating horror, I questioned what had happened. Was it about having too much money? Untreated mental illness? I wondered when logic and shame might kick in—when someone might get him to stop. But the more he was rejected by his peers, the media, and some fans, the more Kanye seemed to act out. Eventually, I accepted, grimly, that I was watching someone who, feeling abandoned and misunderstood, was determined to ignore all of his critics and double down on pursuing his chosen path.

I thought about Ye while I was reading The Castle, a new nonfiction work by the journalist Jon Ronson that attempts to unpack the motivations of wayward men who no longer fit into traditional society. Ronson is probably best-known for his 2015 book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed, a journalistic account of the emotional incentives and historical context behind the social-media-fueled frenzy that became known as “cancel culture.” Like the people in that book, many of the subjects of The Castle have been shoved to the margins. But the forces at play in this new book are more disparate, and perhaps more stubborn, than an angry online mob. Ronson explores how men become alienated because they can’t achieve success in their chosen field, because they can’t pay their bills, because they have too much money, because the town around them went to hell. The book shows how their free will, coupled with a lot of free time on the internet, leads them to pursue their self-interest as best they can—which, eventually, begets more alienation.

The Castle opens with the story of a strange encounter with a strange man. One night in 2023, Ronson’s 20-something son, Joel, and three of his friends (two are women) are invited to a mysterious castle in the middle of nowhere—specifically, Woodstock, Connecticut—for what they believe is a party. There, the women are asked to participate in a bizarre dating show hosted by a man named Chris Mark. The idea is apparently that 101 women will dress up like princesses and vie to be Mark’s girlfriend; once the situation becomes predictably awkward, Mark seemingly deems the night a bust and kicks everyone out. Ronson, who wakes up to a slew of texts from Joel describing what happened, is alarmed by the whole episode—and decides he needs to meet Mark himself.

On their first meeting, Mark at first seems transparent about how he spends his time. He owns the castle, where he lives with several women whom he met online. The entire scene strikes Ronson as reminiscent of Hugh Hefner’s grotto—an analogy they discuss at Ronson’s prompting. But Mark, in Ronson’s telling, quickly grows antagonistic, abruptly asking Ronson to sign an NDA, then later barraging him with suspicious texts and threatening him with a pair of goons. Ronson concludes that Mark has “nurtured a private fantasy of manhood” that the journalist has put at risk by asking questions. (Mark has contested many of the details and claims of The Castle, including that he sent anyone to threaten Ronson, and has said that Ronson “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner.”)

The Castle is about both Ronson’s investigation into Mark and the bigger phenomenon Mark seems to represent: too-idle men, most of them less wealthy than Mark, littering the country, yearning for some kind of grander purpose. He’s especially interested in men ages 25 to 54 who are both unemployed and no longer looking for work—people he claims have “opted out of society,” choosing instead a “life of male nothingness.” In a moment of general anxiety about men—whom they vote for, what they’re reading, whether they share their feelings—his interest isn’t political. It’s empathic. He offers no prescriptive solutions, wags no fingers. Instead, he wants the reader to conceive of the scale of social anomie, and to envision the millions of other men chasing meaning in the wreckage of their former aspirations.

In particular, Ronson focuses on a demographic whose life expectancy has dropped in the 21st century: middle-aged white men without college degrees, many of whom suffer from what a pair of Princeton economists he speaks with define as “deaths of despair” brought on by “the erosion of a way of life.” Once upon a time, such men—who widely supported Donald Trump in all three of his runs for president—were sold on the American dream. Now some of them are characterized by “a kind of cowed, vaguely shocked hopelessness,” Ronson writes. Others, facing social rejection, have started to live “like separatists, creating worlds in which they didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on their own terms.” Women, too, suffer from deaths of despair—but it’s the men, Ronson indicates, who have been raised to envision themselves as heroes, a self-image that can drive them to dark places.

Ronson illustrates how easy it can be for these men to slide off the map. His most endearing subject is Greg Chism, a father of two daughters in small-town Illinois. Chism was a single parent with tons of medical debt living in a place without a lot of job opportunities when, in the 2010s, he discovered a YouTube channel encouraging viewers to “make a video and change your life.” A few of his early videos got some attention, after which Chism received coaching from the platform’s employees, and he eventually struck on a winning formula: bizarre sketches involving his two daughters that played like the output of a hallucinating LLM fed on Nickelodeon. These generated millions of views, and some of them got really weird; Chism and his kids dressed like babies, or pretended to eat cat food off pizza. Soon came the blowback: Chism was, the internet claimed, a bad father abusing his children by making them participate in these creepy videos. His channel was demonetized, then banned. He was shunned just as quickly as he’d been celebrated.

But Chism, whom Ronson tracks down, has not been radicalized by the wave of hatred that came his way. Nor does he seem to be a bad father; his (now teenage) kids express mostly fond memories of their channel. He admits making errors in judgment—see: cat food—but in the end, Ronson writes, Chism was “a single father juggling responsibilities while feeling foolishly idealistic about sharing his family’s lives on the internet.” Becoming a YouTuber had seemed like a way for Chism to stop sliding toward destitution. Instead, his entire life was put under a microscope. Ronson uses Chism’s guilelessness to show how unexpected and profound the pitfalls can be for anyone looking to find a foothold in the new world.

So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed examined a group of people whose lives were ruined by the internet in one particular way; The Castle flips the framing. In the latter book’s view, the internet allows its users to choose their own particular off-ramp from ennui. Seeking female companionship, Chris Mark turns to dating apps; eager to feel seen, Greg Chism becomes a YouTuber. One subject, the podcaster Andrew Gold, begins tailoring his content to anti-woke audiences, racking up huge numbers by playing to the preexisting grievances of his angry followers. Another chapter digs into Ronson’s rocky friendship with the comedy writer Graham Linehan, whose involvement in the gender-critical movement led him to act out online in ways that Ronson reads as self-destructive. (Linehan has disputed many of the details of Ronson’s depiction, and called it “an indictment of him and the cowardly, careerist, mendacious class of people who could roughly gather under the title ‘Graham Linehan’s old friends and colleagues.’”)

A swerve comes toward the end when Ronson wonders whether he has fallen into the same trap as some of those men. By treating Mark’s story as something only he can make sense of, Ronson has neglected his friends and his marriage. “Everyone I met for this book had, I thought, a similarly dysfunctional relationship with purpose, hunting too desperately for it,” he writes. “And now there was a generation of men, unanchored from society and going it alone—as content creators, culture war influencers, amateur sleuths.”

Ronson doesn’t build toward any prescriptive conclusions; he gives these men a platform to explain how they feel, and allows the reader to weigh the validity of those feelings. I remember the Chism pile-on well, and was slightly horrified to hear the story from his perspective—how confusing it must have felt to toggle so rapidly and randomly between being seen as heroic and villainous. Ronson’s empathy is not boundless; he draws hard lines around some of Mark’s behavior. But he seems to understand that his personal judgment is more or less meaningless. The factors shaping these men are external, but how they react comes from the inside—and many of them remain trapped in their own metaphorical castles, far from the light.

entries.title: Americans Don’t Understand Who’s Rich
entries.summary: The small-business owners with curiously large fortunes
entries.content:
Terry Taylor is worth about $2 billion, and you have almost surely never heard of him. Based in Florida, he doesn’t put his name on the car dealerships that he buys up, and he reportedly attends conferences only on the condition that no one announces who he is. Taylor came to our attention in 2023, when he paid $76 million for an Aspen mansion—then the most expensive home sale in the Colorado town’s history.

In 2024, Forbes magazine, which keeps tabs on the richest people in the United States and around the world, slotted Taylor in at No. 1,694 on its World Billionaires List and published a profile titled “The Car Dealership Billionaire No One Knows.” “He’s like Batman,” a source told Forbes. “You hear about him and you admire his work, but nobody has really ever seen him in real life.”

When Americans picture the ultrarich, they typically think of tech billionaires such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, whose wealth lies predominantly in shares of publicly traded companies. They might also think of Wall Street financiers and celebrities such as Taylor Swift. But far more typical are figures like Terry Taylor—which is to say, owners of successful privately held businesses. We are economists who have been studying taxation and inequality for more than a decade. By our calculations, about 1.7 million Americans have each built a net worth of at least $10 million by owning a private business. For every CEO of a public company, there are more than 1,000 private-business owners with a net worth of more than $25 million.

In the course of our research, we’ve come to call these people “everywhere millionaires” because they exist all around the country, in a huge range of industries. Perhaps not surprising, some of these millionaires have stakes in investment firms or medical, dental, or legal practices. But the ranks of everywhere millionaires also include a repo man from Henderson, Nevada; a car-wash owner from Milwaukee; a treated-lumber magnate from Alabama; a boat-cover maker from the Ozarks.

What we found changed how we think about inequality. During the Occupy Wall Street protests after the 2008 financial crisis, the prototypical one-percenters were executives at big banks. Today, when Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders propose making the rich pay their fair share, they aim at Wall Street and Silicon Valley. But far more relevant to the story of inequality in America are the everywhere millionaires who quietly press their elected representatives for favorable treatment. The tax code bears their imprint far more than it does Musk’s.

Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for example, gutted the electric-vehicle and clean-energy credits, to the Tesla CEO’s detriment. The same bill made permanent a 20 percent deduction that effectively lowers the top tax rate for private-business owners from 37 percent to 30 percent. And it preserved a loophole that lets business owners in most of the country, but not salaried employees, deduct their state and local taxes in full.

When asked on Meet the Press why the cut for the highest earners had to be permanent, House Speaker Mike Johnson said: “This is not giving tax cuts to millionaires; it’s the opposite. The people in the tax bracket that you’re referring to, many of them are small-business owners.” Although many top-bracket taxpayers do indeed own businesses, the benefits of these provisions flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest among them.

A loophole that lets private-business owners avoid Medicare taxes has similarly been justified as a break for the little guy. Preserving the family farm has been a pretext for passing ever larger exemptions to the estate tax, to the point that a married couple can now pass on $30 million to heirs tax-free. Hiding behind small business, in short, has proved a devastatingly effective strategy for the rich.

The financial affairs of some of the wealthiest Americans have long been opaque. The Forbes 400 began in 1982 at the direction of the publisher Malcolm Forbes, who reportedly had been inspired by the ballroom capacity at the New York socialite Caroline Astor’s Fifth Avenue mansion. At the time, editorial staffers doubted they could find the 400 richest people, let alone measure their wealth. Although for public companies, people who own a large number of shares must disclose their holdings, and the compensation of top executives is a matter of public record, many wealthy owners of privately held businesses closely guard details about their finances. Kerry Dolan, a Forbes editor, told The New York Times in 2022 that the magazine’s search for billionaires might never pick up on someone who had quietly made $250 million from selling a stake in a business and had invested the proceeds well.

The U.S. government’s view into this world is similarly limited. The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances includes a supplemental sample of a few hundred ultrarich respondents. Tracking down even this small number of people requires an expert staff to conduct interviews and a budget of tens of millions of dollars, a survey official told us. Only one in 10 who are contacted cooperates with the survey. The IRS collects voluminous confidential information about businesses and their owners. But it’s stored in a labyrinth of separate systems and databases, making it hard for anyone to use it to answer even basic questions: How many private-business owners are there across the United States? How rich are they, and how did they become rich? Without detailed information on how privately held businesses operate and make money, experts cannot estimate the effects of tax changes and other policies.

After the two of us finished graduate school in 2014, we worked as unpaid analysts for the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Tax Analysis. Along with our friend Danny Yagan, we were assigned a project to help the department figure out how much tax various categories of business owners were paying, and we were given a database of anonymized records to analyze. (For research purposes, each taxpayer is assigned a unique identification number. The names and actual tax IDs of the businesses and individuals who submit tax forms are confidential; the IRS cannot legally disclose them even to other parts of the government.) By combining various data sets over the course of months, we could fill out a detailed map of American enterprise and observe how business owners build their fortunes.

Even without knowing owners’ names, we learned a lot: We were able to cross-reference the tax data with anonymized data sets from past research containing standardized-test scores, parental income, and early-career trajectories. This information became the statistical foundation for a series of research papers.

The more we came to recognize the importance of everywhere millionaires, the more we wanted to understand their decision making. So we sought to identify some through public sources and tell their stories. We looked, for instance, at trade publications that ranked top earners. We interviewed industry experts and combed through databases such as Dun & Bradstreet, which collects reams of information about businesses and their leaders. We also tapped our own networks.

The more people we told about our quest to find rich private-business owners, the more leads we gathered. A family member from St. Louis pointed us to the Tracy family, who owns Dot Foods—the nation’s largest food redistributor, which generates more than $10 billion in revenue a year and was started from the back of a station wagon by a dairy farmer and his wife, Dorothy, in rural Illinois. Some of the most memorable businesses we came across were the least glamorous. One was a regional distributor of garbage trucks, street sweepers, and sewer suckers for municipalities.

Once we identified the top earners in an industry, we learned more about them through public information, such as newspaper and magazine profiles and published memoirs. Property records for luxury homes and registries of private-jet and yacht owners pointed us to colorful stories. We traced a 100-foot yacht moored off Manhattan Beach to the founder of Bird Barrier, a company that keeps pigeons off buildings. A 383-foot yacht belonged to the man who built Harbor Freight Tools, the discount-tool chain. Others were owned by a forklift manufacturer in New Bremen, Ohio; a Long Island scrap-metal recycler; and a slew of auto dealers.

Whatever they sell—cars, treated lumber, boat covers—the everywhere millionaires have one thing in common: They own what have become known as pass-through businesses because their profits skip the traditional corporate tax entirely and flow straight to owners, to be taxed at the individual rate. This structure surged in popularity following the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which cut the top individual tax rate to less than the corporate tax rate for the first time in U.S. history. In the decades since, lawmakers have carved out multiple loopholes, so a dollar earned from owning a business is routinely taxed much less than a dollar earned in wages. Moreover, business owners have a far greater ability to underreport their income to the IRS than wealthy CEOs do.

In some sense, getting rich by starting a business is an old American story, but the rise of education-dependent knowledge industries has gotten much more attention in the past few decades. When we were graduating from college, we were drawn to what many American middle-class families have come to see as the conventional paths to prosperity: tech and finance. Eric worked for a time as a software developer in a few start-ups, and Owen as an analyst at a venture-capital firm. But our subsequent economic research showed that studying, going to good schools, and then landing a job working at a prestigious company was hardly the only way to get ahead.

In the upper reaches of the wealth distribution, the advantages of entrepreneurship appear stark. According to our analysis of the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the 65,000 American households worth more than $100 million consisted almost entirely of business owners; fewer than half held graduate degrees. When we matched entrepreneurs with their test scores, we found that people with average SAT results were more likely to build a highly successful business than to make a comparable fortune as a salaried worker. Owning, it turns out, often beats earning.

But for all the benefits of entrepreneurial risk-taking, everywhere millionaires are also the beneficiaries of U.S. government policy, which they shape to their advantage.

As Congress drafted the 2017 tax law—which ultimately became the biggest business-tax cut in history—we met an auto dealer who had become a member of Congress and warned that the bill would devastate his industry. Dealers borrow heavily to keep cars on the lot. To help offset the tax cuts, the proposed bill limited how much interest businesses could deduct. By the time the bill passed, though, auto dealers had won a special exemption from that limit.

Once you start watching for favors like this, you see these business owners’ influence everywhere: in tax legislation, in market regulation (or the lack thereof), and in the backgrounds of candidates for elected office. Everywhere millionaires don’t get the same attention as eccentric tech titans, finance executives, or famous entertainers. But seeing them is the first step to understanding the economy and society as they really are.
